title: The Planet's Ledger
objectives: I can use ten words to describe how people use, protect, and harm natural resources.
I can tell the two meanings of exhaust, degrade, and exploit apart by reading the context.
I can explain the difference between a finite resource and a renewable one.
I can write a short argument about environmental responsibility using at least four words from this unit.
rationale: Environmental texts are dense with precise verbs of use and loss, and the same words show up in science, social studies and the news. The ten words give students the vocabulary of resources (finite, renewable, emission, extinct), the verbs of damage (exhaust, degrade, exploit), and the words for care and repair (conservation, stewardship, mitigate). Exhaust, degrade and exploit each have a second sense that students already know from everyday life, so the unit teaches them to choose a sense from context. The passage frames the planet as a ledger to make the idea of balance concrete, and the unit sets up the consequences unit that follows.

words.def: Careful, responsible management of something you are trusted to look after, such as land or natural resources.
words.ex: The farmers' stewardship of the river included planting trees along the bank to keep the soil in place.

passage.title: The Planet's Ledger
paras: Imagine the planet as a ledger, a book that records what we take and what we give back. For most of history, people drew from it as if the balance could never run out. Today we know that many entries are finite. Oil, coal, and natural gas formed over millions of years, and we are using them far faster than nature can replace them.

When a resource is used carelessly, the damage takes several forms. Farmers who plant the same crop year after year can exhaust the soil, leaving it too poor to grow anything. Fields stripped of plants can degrade, losing topsoil that took centuries to build. Some species have been exploited until they vanished. The passenger pigeon, once among the most numerous birds in North America, was hunted so heavily that it became extinct. The last one, named Martha, died in a zoo in Cincinnati in 1914.

Burning fossil fuels also changes the air. The emissions of carbon dioxide from cars, factories, and power plants trap heat in the atmosphere, and most climate scientists agree that this is warming the planet.

Responses come in three kinds. Conservation means using resources carefully so that they last, whether by repairing instead of replacing or by protecting forests and wetlands. Renewable energy, such as wind and solar power, draws on sources that nature replaces constantly. And some actions mitigate harm that has already begun. Planting trees, restoring wetlands, and building homes that waste less heat reduce the damage even when it cannot be undone.

Behind all of these is stewardship, the idea that people are caretakers of something they did not create and cannot replace. A steward does not ask, “What can I take?” but “What am I leaving behind?” In the end, the ledger has to balance.

qs.q: In paragraph 2, the word “exhaust” most nearly means
choices: make very tired
use up completely
clean thoroughly
save for later
qs.why: The sentence says farmers can leave the soil too poor to grow anything, which means they use up its nutrients. The sense of tiredness does not fit the soil.

qs.q: Why does the author compare the planet to a ledger?
choices: To show that the planet is full of old books
To argue that businesses should keep better records
To prove that most resources will never run out
To suggest that people should weigh what they take against what they give back
qs.why: A ledger records what comes in and what goes out, and the ending says the ledger has to balance.

qs.q: Which sentence best shows that human activity can cause a species to become extinct?
choices: The passenger pigeon was hunted so heavily that it became extinct.
Oil, coal, and natural gas formed over millions of years.
Fields stripped of plants can lose their topsoil.
Emissions of carbon dioxide trap heat in the atmosphere.
qs.why: The passenger pigeon example links human hunting directly to the loss of the whole species.

qs.q: According to paragraph 4, how does mitigation differ from conservation?
choices: Mitigation is done by governments, while conservation is done by farmers.
Mitigation replaces fossil fuels, while conservation only protects animals.
Mitigation reduces harm that has already begun, while conservation aims to use resources carefully so they last.
Mitigation makes harm worse, while conservation makes it better.
qs.why: The paragraph describes mitigation as reducing damage that has started and conservation as careful use that helps resources last.

qs.q: Which statement best expresses the main idea of the passage?
choices: Renewable energy will soon replace every kind of fuel.
Because many resources are limited, people should act as caretakers who weigh what they take against what they leave.
Only governments can protect natural resources.
Extinction is a natural process that people cannot influence.
qs.why: The passage moves from limits and damage to responses and closes on stewardship and a balanced ledger.

teacher.overview: Students learn ten words for talking precisely about resources, loss, and care, with three multiple-meaning verbs (exhaust, degrade, exploit) that need context to read. They practice the difference between finite and renewable, add noun suffixes (-ation, -ship) and prefixes (re-, de-, e-), and read an informational passage that treats the planet as a ledger. The unit connects to ethics, accountability and proliferation earlier in the year and leads into the consequences unit.

notes.va.stewardship.n: Stewardship is careful management of something you are trusted with. It is steward plus -ship. Ask students to name something they are a steward of, such as a classroom library or a pet. Avoid moralizing; ask what a steward owes to others.
notes.va.conservation.n: Conservation is careful use and protection. Students may confuse it with preservation; in this unit the difference is minor, and teachers can mention that preservation often means leaving something untouched. The verb is conserve, and the final e drops before -ation.
notes.va.exhaust.v: Exhaust has two senses: use up completely (taught) and make very tired (shown as a second sense). In context, ask whether the object is a supply or a person. The noun exhaust (fumes) is a third use; mention it only if students raise it.
notes.va.renewable.adj: Renewable is re- plus new plus -able. Many students think renewable means unlimited; clarify that a renewable resource can still be overused. Ask students to sort sources of energy into renewable and finite.
notes.va.emission.n: Emission is e- (out) plus miss (send) plus -ion, a sending-out. Students may hear it as only a car word; extend to factories, farms and volcanoes. Make sure students name what is emitted.
notes.va.extinct.adj: Extinct means no living members remain. Contrast with endangered and threatened. The passenger pigeon and the dodo are well-documented examples of species lost partly because of human activity. Be careful with the word for species that are only rare.
notes.va.finite.adj: Finite means having a limit. Its opposite is infinite. Students may think finite means small; a finite number can be enormous. Use time and fresh water as everyday examples.
notes.va.degrade.v: Degrade has two senses: make worse in condition (taught) and treat a person without dignity (shown as a second sense). The prefix de- (down) is a clue. Ask students what degraded land looks like and how it could be restored.
notes.va.exploit.v: Exploit has two senses: use unfairly (taught) and make full use of (shown as a second sense). The negative sense is tied to harm and unfairness. Ask students to decide which sense each sentence uses and to point out the context clue.
notes.va.mitigate.v: Mitigate means to lessen a harm. Students often confuse it with mediate or with prevent. Use the test: is the harm still coming? Then mitigate. Is the harm stopped entirely? Then prevent. Ask for mitigation of a harm in the community.

teacher.model: Think-aloud: “The passage says the soil can be exhausted. Is that use up or make tired? Soil cannot get tired, so it means use up. Oil is finite, so it can be exhausted, but wind is renewable. Planting trees does not stop the heat, but it can mitigate it. That is the difference between prevent and mitigate.”

teacher.reviewAdvice: Bring back accountable, ethical and proliferate when students discuss who is responsible for harm to the environment. Revisit exhaust, degrade and exploit after two days with new sentences where students must choose a sense, and use mitigate and exploit again in the consequences unit.

Fact claims to confirm: oil, coal and natural gas formed over millions of years; the passenger pigeon was once among the most numerous birds in North America, was overhunted, and the last one (Martha) died at the Cincinnati Zoo in 1914; the dodo lived on Mauritius and has been extinct for centuries; the woolly mammoth became extinct thousands of years ago; electric cars have no tailpipe emissions; most climate scientists agree that carbon dioxide emissions are warming the planet.
Morphology: emission segmented as e- + miss + -ion (spelling documented in the note); degrade segmented as de- + grade with a plain-language gloss; confirm against an etymology source.
Sense boundaries: exhaust, degrade and exploit are each taught in one sense with a second sense shown.
